package.name: Io
package.description: Streams, console I/O, readers and writers

modules.name: Binary
modules.header:
Binary values on a byte stream, with the byte order named rather than assumed.
A file format or a wire protocol fixes its byte order once, in its specification, and every machine that reads
it honors that choice regardless of its own. So every function here takes the order as an argument: the caller
names the format's choice, and the code assembles values arithmetically — shift and or, never a reinterpreted
memory read — so the host's own order never enters into it.
One pair of word functions does the actual work at every width, accumulating in the widest integer there is;
the typed functions are the surface, one per primitive width, so a format description reads as what it stores.
Floats travel as the IEEE 754 bit patterns of their width, moved between integer and float representation
without conversion.

modules.name: Buffered
modules.header:
Buffering: fewer, larger conversations with the machine.
A system call costs the same for one byte as for four thousand, so a program that reads or writes in small
pieces pays the call's price per piece. The buffered reader and writer stand between, turning many small
operations into few large ones — and both step aside for operations already larger than the buffer, where
copying through it would only add work. They keep interface values because their streams must be stored;
call-time helpers elsewhere take borrowed interface references instead.
The close contracts differ, and the difference is the design. A reader abandoned mid-buffer loses nothing
anybody asked for. A writer abandoned mid-buffer holds bytes the caller believes are written, so its destructor
flushes — but a destructor has nowhere to report failure, so the flush's outcome is discarded there. The
explicit `Flush` is where errors are seen, and a caller who cares calls it; the destructor is the safety net,
not the contract.

modules.name: IoError
modules.header:
What went wrong at the edge of the machine.
An I/O failure is not one thing. Some report a fact about the world — the file is not there, the disk is full,
permission was refused — and a caller acts on which fact. Some report a moment: the operation was interrupted,
or would block, and the right response is to go again. And the end of a stream is not a failure at all, but it
arrives through the same channel, so it lives in the same type where nobody can lose it.
The set is deliberately the meanings shared by every platform, with the raw code carried beside the meaning:
translation loses detail, and the detail is sometimes the diagnosis. Success is not in the set: an operation that
can fail returns a native fallible, and `IoError` is only ever its failure.

modules.name: Print
modules.header:
Printing, with the failure a caller can act on returned rather than swallowed.
Every overload returns the `IoError` of the write it made, or `none` when there was nothing to report. Most call
sites will keep ignoring it, and that is their decision rather than this module's: a program logging to a terminal
loses nothing by not looking, while one whose output feeds a closed pipe has something to look at. That is why the
result is an optional failure rather than a fallible, which a statement could not leave unread. The bytes go
through the standard output handle, so the console-versus-redirection encoding is decided where it always is, not
re-decided here.

modules.name: PrintLine
modules.header:
The line-ending variants: the value, then a newline, with the first failure returned.
The newline is written only when the value's own write succeeded. That used to be unconditional, which meant a
line whose value could not be written still moved the cursor — so a program logging into a pipe that had
closed emitted a run of empty lines, and one whose value was refused for a bad request emitted a line with
nothing on it. Neither is what the caller asked for: a line is the value and its terminator together, and half
of one is worse than none of it.
One helper decides that for every overload rather than each repeating the rule. There are twenty-two of them,
and a rule written twenty-two times is a rule that will be written wrongly once.

modules.name: ReadLine
modules.header:
Reading a line typed at the process, through the standard input handle.
This is the console companion to `ReadTextLine`, with the same line contract: a line feed ends the line, a
carriage return immediately before it belongs to the ending, the last line needs no ending, and the line is
UTF-8. It is read byte by byte, so nothing past the line is taken from a stream that may be shared. The bytes come
through `StandardIn`, so typed input on a Windows console arrives as correct UTF-8 rather than code-page text.
`ReadLineFrom` is the same reading over any `Reader`, which is also what lets the contract be tested without a
console.

modules.name: Standard
modules.header:
The three streams every process is born holding, as byte streams with the encoding question answered once.
Nothing here is opened and nothing is closed: stdin, stdout and stderr belong to the process, not to any value
in it, and a handle that closed them on drop would take them from every other part of the program. What
acquisition does own is the answer to a question that must not be asked per write: whether the stream is a
console. On Windows that decides the encoding — a console wants UTF-16 through its own entry points, while a
redirected stream wants the raw UTF-8 bytes on disk exactly as written — and deciding it per operation would
put a system call in front of every one. Elsewhere the bytes are the bytes, console or not.

modules.name: Stream
modules.header:
The three things a stream can be asked, and the helpers every asker shares.
A `Reader` fills what it can of a buffer and succeeds with how much; a `Writer` takes what it can and succeeds with
how much; a `Seeker` moves the position and succeeds with where it landed. Partial progress is the interfaces'
honest unit — a socket hands over what has arrived, a pipe takes what fits — and the all-or-nothing shapes callers
usually want are the shared helpers, written once: `ReadExact` and `WriteAll` loop over partial progress, retry the
transient reports, and refuse to spin on a stream that makes none.
Call-time streams are borrowed as interface references, so concrete readers and writers can be used directly
without copying their state or manufacturing an adapter. An interface value is still useful when a stream must
be stored, because references deliberately cannot escape into fields.

modules.name: TextBoundary
modules.header:
Where a stream and the text protocols meet, and what each says to the other.
`Rux/Text` describes values and knows nothing about streams; this package moves bytes and knows nothing about
rendering. They have to agree at exactly one place — a `TextWriter` over a stream — and the whole difficulty is
that neither error type can hold the other's failures. `FormatError` has one case for a destination failing,
`WriterFailure`, with deliberately no room for details, because Text has no vocabulary for a broken pipe and
should not pretend to. `IoError` has no case for a placeholder that does not parse.
So the crossing is made in both directions, once, here.
Going out, `FromIoError` turns what a stream reported into what a formatter understands: success stays success
and every failure becomes `WriterFailure`. That is lossy on purpose, and the loss is made good by the adapter,
which records the original `IoError` in an optional slot the caller holds. So the formatter learns exactly what it
can act on — stop writing — and the caller learns exactly what happened.
Coming back, `ToIoError` turns a formatting failure into something a stream's caller can act on, and the one
distinction it must preserve is the one that decides what to do next: a destination that failed may be worth
retrying elsewhere, while a request that was wrong will be wrong again. A malformed pattern, a specification a
value does not support, an argument count that does not match, and a value outside the form asked for are all
the caller's own request, and all arrive as `InvalidInput`. Text that was not valid UTF-8 is `InvalidText`, which
is a fact about the bytes. A bounded destination that filled up is `LimitExceeded`. This used to be one line
mapping everything to `InvalidText`, which told a caller who had written `{:q}` that their bytes were not text.
What is *not* done is stuffing a `FormatError` into `IoError`'s `raw` field. That field is `errno` on the Unix
systems and the Win32 code on Windows, and a caller reading it expects to be able to look the number up. A
caller who needs to know which formatting failure it was builds a `ConsoleWriter` — or any other `TextWriter` —
and calls `Text::WriteValue` themselves, which hands back the `FormatError` whole.

modules.name: TextRead
modules.header:
Reading text out of a byte stream, a line at a time.
A line ends at a line feed, and a carriage return immediately before it belongs to the ending, not the line --
that one rule is the whole of newline normalization, and it makes files from either lineage read the same. A
carriage return anywhere else is content: the platform that ended lines with it alone has been gone thirty
years, and treating every stray CR as an ending would corrupt honest text to accommodate a ghost.
The bound is not advice. A caller reading lines from an untrusted stream names the longest line it will hold,
and a longer one is `LimitExceeded` rather than a slow exhaustion of memory: unbounded line reading from a
socket is how a peer that never sends a newline takes the process down.

doc.summary: Appends the next line of standard input to `builder`, without its ending.
doc.markdown:
Appends the next line of standard input to `builder`, without its ending.
`EndOfStream` is reported only when the input ends with nothing before it; a stream failure is returned as
itself, with whatever was read so far left in the builder. The line must be UTF-8: a byte that does not belong
to a well-formed character, or a character cut short by the end of the input, is `InvalidText`, reported once
the rest of the line has been read through its ending so that the next call starts on the next line; the text
before the fault stays in the builder. Reads one byte at a time on purpose: standard input may be shared with
whatever runs next, and a buffer here would take bytes that were never this line's.

to the ending, and `EndOfStream` is reported only when the source ends with nothing before it. A stream failure
is returned as itself, with whatever was read so far left in the builder. The line must be UTF-8: a byte that
does not belong to a well-formed character, or a character cut short by the end of the source, is
`InvalidText`, reported once the rest of the line has been read through its ending; the text before the fault
stays in the builder. No byte past the line's ending is read, which is what makes it safe on a shared stream;
a source that is not shared reads faster through `ReadTextLine` over a `BufferedReader`.

doc.summary: Turns what a stream reported into what a formatter understands.
doc.markdown:
Turns what a stream reported into what a formatter understands.
Success becomes the formatter's success value; every failure becomes `WriterFailure`, which is the only thing
`FormatError` can say about a destination. The details do not travel this way — an adapter records the original
`IoError` where its caller can read it, which is what keeps the loss from being a loss.
The end of a stream is a failure here. Nothing is being read, so a write that reports it is a destination that
cannot take the bytes, whatever it calls that.
doc.returns: success for a success, and `WriterFailure` for any failure

doc.summary: Turns a formatting failure into something a stream's caller can act on.
doc.markdown:
Turns a formatting failure into something a stream's caller can act on.
The distinction that survives is the one worth having: a request that was wrong is `InvalidInput` and will be
wrong again, while a destination that failed came back as an `IoError` in the first place and never reaches
here. Bytes that were not text are `InvalidText`; a bounded destination that filled is `LimitExceeded`.
`WriterFailure` should not arrive: an adapter records the stream's own error and its caller reports that
instead. It maps to `Other` rather than being ignored, so an adapter that forgets to keep the original is
visibly wrong rather than quietly reporting success.
doc.returns: the closest I/O meaning, with no platform code, since none applies

doc.summary: A `TextWriter` over standard output that records the stream's failure where the caller can see it.
doc.markdown:
A `TextWriter` over standard output that records the stream's failure where the caller can see it.
The protocol has one case for a destination failing, `WriterFailure`, and deliberately no room for the details:
Text has no vocabulary for a broken pipe and does not pretend to. So this adapter keeps both halves. It reports
`WriterFailure` to the formatter, which stops the write, and records the original `IoError` in the slot it was
built over, which is what the caller reads afterwards. Nothing about the stream failure is lost, and nothing
about it leaks into a package that could not interpret it. The slot starts as `none`, and holds the failure once
there is one.
The slot must outlive the writer. It is a stored address, so nothing here tracks that.

doc.markdown:
A writer over standard output, recording into `failure`.
The slot is read before every write as well as written on failure, so a writer built over a slot that
already holds a failure writes nothing at all.

doc.summary: Writes `bytes` to standard output.
doc.markdown:
Writes `bytes` to standard output.
Reports `WriterFailure` when the stream refuses, having recorded the original `IoError` in the slot. Once a
failure has been recorded every later write is refused without touching the stream, so a value that is
part-way through rendering does not go on writing into a handle that has already failed, and a trailing
newline is not emitted after a failed line. This is the only case this writer can produce: the bytes are not
revalidated, and standard output is not a bounded destination.
doc.returns: success when the stream accepted the whole run

doc.summary: A `TextWriter` over any stream, recording the stream's failure where the caller can see it.
doc.markdown:
A `TextWriter` over any stream, recording the stream's failure where the caller can see it.
The same two halves as `ConsoleWriter`, over a destination the caller chose: a file, a buffered writer, a pipe.
It is what lets a value describe itself into a stream at all — `Display` writes into a `TextWriter` and a stream
takes bytes, and until something stands between them a value can only be rendered to standard output or into
memory.
Whole runs go out through `WriteAll`, so a stream that takes a partial write is looped over rather than losing
the rest of a value's text.
The slot must outlive the writer. It is a stored address, so nothing here tracks that.

doc.summary: A text writer over `sink`, recording into `failure`.
doc.markdown:
A text writer over `sink`, recording into `failure`.
`sink` is borrowed for the call and kept. The slot is read before every write as well as written on failure,
so a writer built over a slot that already holds a failure writes nothing at all.

params.name: failure
params.markdown: where the first stream failure is recorded, `none` until there is one

doc.returns: a text writer over that stream

members.name: Write
members.signature: pub func Write(self: &var StreamWriter, bytes: char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `bytes` to the stream.
doc.markdown:
Writes `bytes` to the stream.
Reports `WriterFailure` when the stream refuses, having recorded the original `IoError` in the slot. Once a
failure has been recorded every later write is refused without touching the stream, so a value part-way
through rendering does not go on writing into a destination that has already failed.
doc.returns: success when the stream accepted the whole run

items.name: WriteValueLine
items.signature: pub func WriteValueLine<T: Display>(writer: &var TextWriter, value: &T) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes a value's text, then a newline, and writes the newline only if the value went out whole.
doc.markdown:
Writes a value's text, then a newline, and writes the newline only if the value went out whole.
The rule is the whole point. A line is a value and its terminator together, so a value that could not be written
must not be followed by a terminator: a destination that refused halfway would otherwise get a line break
marking the end of something that is not there, and a caller reading the output back would see a blank line
where a value should be. This is what every `PrintLine` overload does over standard output, written once for any
destination.
The value is taken by bound rather than as an interface value, and that is the difference between writing a
value and taking it: binding a move-only value to a `Display` transfers ownership of it, so a surface that
accepted one could write such a value exactly once and the caller would not have it afterwards. Here it is
borrowed, so it may be written as often as wanted and is still the caller's.
Reports the value's own failure when it has one, without attempting the newline. Otherwise reports whatever the
newline's write reported.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: the value's type, which must know how to show itself

params.name: value
params.markdown: the value to write, borrowed for the call

doc.returns: success when both the value and the newline were accepted

items.name: WriteFormatLine
items.signature: pub func WriteFormatLine(writer: &var TextWriter, #Format() format: char8[..], ...) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes `format` with each `{}` replaced by the next argument, then a newline, on the same rule.
doc.markdown:
Writes `format` with each `{}` replaced by the next argument, then a newline, on the same rule.
The newline goes out only if the whole pattern did, so a pattern that does not parse, an argument count that
does not match and a destination that refused all leave no terminator behind. Nothing is allocated: the
arguments write themselves as they are reached. They arrive as interface values, which is what a variadic can
carry, so a move-only argument goes through `WriteValueLine` instead of through a placeholder.
A literal `format` has its placeholders counted against the arguments while compiling, since it is marked
`#Format()`. Reports the formatting failure when there is one, without attempting the newline. Otherwise reports
whatever the newline's write reported.

params.name: format
params.markdown: the pattern, whose placeholders are filled from the arguments that follow it

doc.returns: success when the whole line was accepted

items.name: ReadTextLine
items.signature: pub func ReadTextLine(reader: &var BufferedReader, builder: &var StringBuilder, limit: uint) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Appends the next line of `reader` to `builder`, without its ending.
doc.markdown:
Appends the next line of `reader` to `builder`, without its ending.
A line ends at a line feed; a carriage return immediately before it is part of the ending. The last line of a
stream needs no ending: what stands before the end is a line, and `EndOfStream` is reported only when the
stream ends with nothing before it, so a caller loops until exactly that.
The line must be UTF-8 — `InvalidText` otherwise, including a sequence cut short by the end of the stream --
and at most `limit` bytes, `LimitExceeded` otherwise. Only validated bytes ever reach the builder, and on
either failure it is cleared and the offending line consumed through its ending, so the caller can report the
line and read on. A scalar value split across the buffer's edge is completed from the next refill, not
condemned: where the buffer happens to end is not a property of the text.

params.name: builder
params.markdown: receives the line, appended to whatever it already holds

params.name: limit
params.markdown: the most bytes to accept before reporting the line too long

doc.returns: success when a line was read; `IsEnd` at the end of input with nothing appended
